parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Count the whole cost of an accepted outcome
parts.body:
A model price list covers only part of an AI workflow. Count input and output usage, repeated calls, retrieval and indexing, hosting, integration, evaluation, observability, support, human review, and rework. Separate one-time build costs from recurring operations. For a comparison of models, keep the workload, quality requirement, and human review policy consistent. A lower token price can be erased by more retries or corrections.

Use cost per successfully completed task as a unit, with a clear definition of success. Divide total relevant operating cost by accepted outcomes, not requests or generated words. Report latency, severe errors, and quality beside cost. A system that defers difficult cases to humans may show high model accuracy because those cases vanished from its denominator; account for them in workflow cost and completion.

Ask the finance and operations owners to validate baseline labour and the value of time released. Hours theoretically saved are not automatically cash savings. If employees use the time for additional work, measure that outcome instead. Keep assumptions visible so the business case can be updated with actual usage.

example.title: A simple unit cost
example.body: In one illustrative month, 10,000 requests incur $2,000 model charges, $700 platform costs, and $3,300 review costs. If 8,000 are accepted, operating cost is $6,000 / 8,000 = $0.75 per accepted task. Build costs and other overhead would need separate treatment.

exercise.title: Build a cost numerator
exercise.body: For a proposed assistant, identify every recurring cost line and its owner. Define a completed task, exclusion, and quality standard. Calculate cost per accepted task with illustrative numbers and list the costs you cannot yet measure.

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Compare options on the same denominator
parts.body:
Suppose a cheaper model saves $500 in calls but reduces accepted tasks from 8,000 to 7,000. If all other operating costs stay at $4,000, its monthly total is $5,500 and cost per accepted task is about $0.79. The earlier option costs $0.75. The cheaper call has a worse unit cost under these assumptions. If the unaccepted tasks require extra staff work, the gap grows. These are teaching figures, not a forecast.

A fair comparison also asks whether the options serve the same case mix. A small model might handle routine questions cheaply while a more capable model receives hard cases. Measure routing errors and the combined path, including two calls when escalation is required. Check p95 latency or another service-level measure for users who experience slow cases; an average can hide their experience.

For procurement, model volume bands, currency exposure, vendor discounts, minimum commitments, data egress, and the cost of switching. The CFO should see a range under low and high demand, not a single point estimate. The CAIO should be able to explain which assumption most changes the decision.

example.title: A smaller price, larger unit cost
example.body: Option A: $6,000 / 8,000 accepted = $0.75. Option B: $5,500 / 7,000 accepted = about $0.79. The cost difference is $0.04 per accepted task before extra repair. The numbers are illustrative and use the same workload.

exercise.title: Run sensitivity cases
exercise.body: Using the example, vary completion rate, review minutes, and monthly volume one at a time. Find the break-even completion rate for Option B at $5,500 total cost against $0.75 per accepted task. State what real-world measurement would settle the choice.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: measurement in context

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Manage latency, capacity, and quality together
parts.body:
Inference capacity is an operating decision. More requests, longer context, larger outputs, and multi-step agents can raise cost and delay. Caching may help repeated, permission-safe content, while routing simple cases to a smaller model can reduce spend. Test these changes against the same acceptance criteria. A cache that serves an obsolete policy or another user's restricted answer creates a new failure.

Set a budget for each workflow, with alerts for changes in requests per task, average context size, retries, and unit cost. Break down cost by team, product, and environment so a test job cannot hide in the production total. Watch latency distributions and queueing at expected peaks. Set explicit behaviour when a provider is unavailable: queue, fall back to a narrower service, or send the case to a person.

Review changes to prompts, retrieval, and models as cost changes as well as quality changes. A new policy corpus may lengthen retrieved context; a longer reasoning path may improve some answers while violating service-time targets. Approve tradeoffs based on business value and risk tier.

example.title: A stale cache decision
example.body: A leave assistant caches answers to save repeated model calls. When HR revises a policy, the cache must expire or be invalidated. The team tests document-version tags and user permissions before counting any savings.

exercise.title: Set an operating alert
exercise.body: Choose cost per accepted task, p95 latency, and one quality measure for a workflow. Give each an owner, observation window, investigation trigger, and action. Add a provider outage path and a stale-cache test.

sources: Google: production ML systems and monitoring

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Present an investment decision with uncertainty
parts.body:
An architecture recommendation should show the expected demand, quality gate, total cost range, cost per accepted task, and the baseline it replaces. Keep the first-year build and migration costs distinct from monthly operations. Include vendor commitments, support, evaluation, and human oversight. State which benefit is realised cash, which is capacity released, and which is a service improvement.

Use scenarios. At low volume, a hosted API may avoid fixed infrastructure cost. At high volume, another deployment may become competitive, but only after allowing for engineering, capacity, and reliability work. Avoid a universal break-even figure; it depends on workload and commercial terms. Include a stop condition if adoption or quality falls below the assumption used to justify investment.

A good board-level summary is brief because its appendix carries the arithmetic. Finance validates labour and spend assumptions, the business owner commits to the outcome, technology validates feasibility, and the CAIO reconciles the evidence across options. Schedule a review after real traffic replaces estimates.

example.title: A decision with a range
example.body: A pilot proposes 2,000 to 8,000 accepted cases per month. The team shows recurring cost per accepted case across that range, expected review hours, first-year setup expense, and a launch gate for answer quality. It chooses a small pilot because volume and correction rates remain uncertain.

exercise.title: Write the finance slide
exercise.body: Draft a one-page comparison of two delivery options and the current process. Include low/base/high volume, accepted outcome definition, all major cost lines, benefit type, severe risk, decision owner, and a three-month review trigger. Label any assumed numbers.
